opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot, because I'd be a bad scientist if I didn't ask what would prove me wrong.

The first thing is the embodiment gap. Human hands and human bodies are very different from robot hardware: different kinematics, different degrees of freedom, different sensing. We feel contact through our skin in ways most robot grippers simply can't. My bet is that a lot of the high-level structure of a task, like what to attend to, what sequence of steps to take, and how objects should move, transfers well from humans to robots. But if it turns out that the hard part of manipulation lives mostly in the low-level physical details, the contact-rich, force-sensitive stuff, then human video alone might not carry as much signal as I hope. You'd still need a lot of robot-specific data to close that gap, and then the "foundation" might really be robot data with human data as a nice-to-have.

The second thing is that the alternatives might scale faster than we expect. If simulation gets good enough, with realistic physics, rendering, and diverse assets generated automatically, you could produce effectively unlimited robot-native data. Or if teleoperation becomes really cheap and fleets of robots are deployed and collecting data in the real world, then the argument that "human data is the only thing abundant enough" gets weaker. Part of my thesis rests on human data being the most scalable source, and that's an empirical claim that could change.

Third, there's the question of whether the data we can actually capture is the right data. Passive internet video is enormous, but it's often missing what matters: precise 3D hand poses, forces, the intent behind an action. Wearable capture systems help, but if it stays hard to get high-quality, well-annotated human data at scale, then you have a lot of quantity but not the right quality.

And finally, there's a possibility I take seriously: maybe the models themselves get so capable, with large world models and video generation models, that they learn the physical priors on their own, and explicitly framing things as "learning from human demonstrations" stops being the right abstraction. In that world human data still matters, but more as part of the general pretraining soup than as a dedicated foundation.

So I'm optimistic, but I hold it as a hypothesis. What I'm watching for is whether we see clear scaling trends, where adding more human data reliably improves robot performance across embodiments. If that curve flattens early, I'll have to update.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation could produce effectively unlimited robot-native data, weakening the case that human data is the most scalable source.

r002.rationale: It describes the embodiment gap and says that if low-level manipulation details dominate, a lot of robot-specific data would be needed to close the gap. This communicates that transfer without substantial robot-specific training may not suffice.

r003.rationale: The response discusses differences between human bodies and robot hardware generally, but does not raise the proliferation of non-humanoid robots as making transfer more difficult.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot, because I don't want to be the person who bet on a direction just because it was convenient.

The biggest thing that could undermine it is the embodiment gap turning out to be more fundamental than I believe it is. My whole premise is that human video, human motion, the way people manipulate objects, contains enough structure about how tasks work that a robot can borrow from it, even though the robot has different hands, different kinematics, different sensing. If it turns out that the useful signal is mostly in the fine-grained contact dynamics, the stuff you can't really observe from the outside, then human data gives you a nice prior for "what to do" but almost nothing about "how to actually do it." And the "how" is where robotics has always been hard. You'd end up with a system that knows it should grasp the mug by the handle but still can't close the loop reliably, and at that point the human data is a bit of a decoration on top of a problem you still have to solve with robot data.

The second thing is scale economics. People sometimes assume human data is free because there's so much video on the internet. But most of that video is terrible for our purposes. It's cut, the camera is moving, you can't see the hands half the time, there's no sense of force or intent. The really useful stuff, egocentric video with good hand visibility, maybe with some pose or contact annotation, that's actually not that cheap to collect at scale either. So if it turns out that robot teleoperation data, which is directly usable, gets cheap faster than useful human data gets collected, then the whole argument flips. You'd just collect robot data because it's the thing you actually need.

And the third one, which I think is underrated, is that the foundation model story might just absorb this problem. If large vision-language models get good enough at understanding physical scenes, task structure, affordances, all of that, then maybe the robot doesn't need human demonstrations as a separate data source. The semantic understanding comes from the pretrained model, and the motor skills come from relatively small amounts of robot data. In that world, human motion data isn't a foundation, it's maybe a fine-tuning signal, or it just gets squeezed out.

What keeps me on this side of the bet is that none of those have really happened yet, and when we look at what actually transfers from human video today, it's more than I would have guessed a few years ago. But I'd be lying if I said I wasn't watching those three things closely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robot teleoperation data becoming cheaper, but does not identify simulation-based learning as a scalability threat.

r002.rationale: It says human data may not capture fine-grained contact skills and that robot data may be needed, but does not specifically identify the human-to-humanoid gap or say transfer with little or no robot-specific training would be impossible.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention a proliferation of non-humanoid robots or its effect on transfer from human data.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing that could undermine that expectation is if the gap between watching humans and controlling a robot turns out to be too hard to bridge. Human video shows you what happened, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you the forces, the contact conditions, or the actions you need to reproduce it with a different body. You can watch someone open a jar and understand the task without knowing how tightly to grip it.

So the question is whether human data actually reduces the amount of robot experience you need. If you train on more and more human data, but the robot still needs essentially the same amount of interaction to learn the task, then that would weaken the argument quite a bit.

The other possibility is that simulation or robot data collection becomes so cheap and scalable that human data is less valuable than we expect. I’d still expect it to help with understanding tasks, but whether it becomes a foundation for learning control is something we have to demonstrate.

r001.rationale: It says simulation or robot data collection could become cheap and scalable enough to make human data less valuable.

r002.rationale: It raises a difficult human-to-robot transfer gap and the possibility that human data will not reduce required robot interaction, but does not specifically identify humanoid robots or clearly say transfer without robot-specific training is impossible.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a proliferation of non-humanoid robots making transfer from human data more difficult.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest uncertainty is the gap between understanding what a human is doing and knowing how a robot should do it. A human video shows you what happened, but it may not tell you the forces, the contacts, or how to recover when something goes wrong. Those details can be essential for manipulation.

So what would change my mind is if we found that, even as we scale human data, the amount of robot experience needed to learn a new task doesn’t really decrease. If the robot still has to learn everything through its own interactions, then human data might be useful for recognizing goals, but much less useful as a foundation for control.

The question is whether human data gives us something transferable that makes robot learning substantially more efficient. I think it can, but that’s the assumption we need to test.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether human data reduces the robot experience needed for learning, but does not mention simulation-based learning or its scalability.

r002.rationale: It raises uncertainty about transferring human data to robot control, but does not identify a human-to-humanoid gap or say transfer with little or no robot-specific training could be impossible.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention non-humanoid robots or their proliferation making transfer more difficult.
